item.text: {"facts":[{"source_id":"SRC-af88723e8ff990bf","start_unit":1,"end_unit":1,"fact_summary":"A 2024 University of Leeds thesis analyzes AMLO’s charismatic leadership as a relational, missionary-populist form of politics, emphasizing his ordinary/extraordinary public persona, faith-based mobilization, and followers’ role in judging congruence between discourse and performance.","question_ids":["4B.2","4B.5","7B.8","8B.1","8B.3"],"polarity":"context","period_fit":"Background analysis of AMLO’s presidency and political style; not specifically limited to 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The thesis is explicitly a case study of Andrés Manuel López Obrador.","limitations":["The supplied unit is an abstract and does not provide 2023-specific policy outcomes or implementation evidence."]},{"source_id":"SRC-b4a0d1404867c381","start_unit":5,"end_unit":5,"fact_summary":"CONEVAL reported that Mexico’s 2022 multidimensional poverty results were based on INEGI’s ENIGH 2022, published July 26, 2023, and were intended to identify barriers to social rights and essential needs and guide coordinated social-policy implementation across government levels.","question_ids":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.5","6B.10","8B.7"],"polarity":"context","period_fit":"2022 outcome data released in 2023; relevant as the latest supplied welfare baseline for 2023.","ruler_attribution":"CONEVAL is Mexico’s state body responsible for multidimensional poverty measurement; the text does not attribute the measurement methodology directly to AMLO.","limitations":["The supplied unit contains no poverty figures, subgroup results, program evaluations, or causal attribution to AMLO’s policies."]},{"source_id":"SRC-07d1ccd98af71f80","start_unit":1,"end_unit":3,"fact_summary":"After Hurricane Otis made landfall as a Category 5 storm on October 25, 2023, AMLO traveled toward Acapulco but was delayed for more than six hours by mud, landslides, blocked roads, and failed vehicle passage; he walked part of the route with security officials, spoke briefly with residents, reached Acapulco around 19:00–19:30, and returned to Mexico City after a short stay while services and an official damage report were not yet fully available.","question_ids":["3B.6","3B.9","6B.6","8B.9"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"Directly concerns a 2023 domestic disaster response.","ruler_attribution":"The report attributes the travel decision, statements, and response actions to AMLO and his cabinet.","limitations":["The report describes access and presence but does not establish the full federal resource allocation, relief outcomes, or whether the return decision caused material harm.","The article reports conflicting or incomplete information about AMLO’s schedule and activities in Acapulco."]},{"source_id":"SRC-29d633396e59a634","start_unit":3,"end_unit":3,"fact_summary":"Amnesty International reported that AMLO proposed reforms in August 2022 to place the National Guard under military control, permit active-duty military personnel to serve without leaving military posts, require military-origin commanders, allow military trials for National Guard personnel accused of international crimes or human-rights violations, and impose military training; Amnesty characterized the militarization as risking further violations and impunity, citing more than 1,100 complaints against the National Guard from 2020–2022 and thousands of complaints involving SEDENA, SEMAR, and the Guard.","question_ids":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.5","3B.6","3B.9","4B.4","8B.2","8B.6","8B.9"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"Policy decisions and complaint figures precede 2023 but describe the security institutional posture inherited into and continuing during 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The proposed reforms are explicitly attributed to President Andrés Manuel López Obrador; the broader complaint data concern Mexican security institutions.","limitations":["The supplied evidence does not establish the final legal status or 2023 implementation details of every proposed reform.","Amnesty’s assessment is an advocacy organization’s characterization, though it cites official complaint figures and international recommendations."]},{"source_id":"SRC-8dca6bca8f63814b","start_unit":20,"end_unit":24,"fact_summary":"The CPJ Mexico archive identifies a 2023 country-document section and provides general navigation and data categories for journalists killed, imprisoned, or missing, but the supplied units contain no specific 2023 incident, count, or assessment.","question_ids":[],"polarity":"context","period_fit":"The supplied material is largely site navigation and does not provide a usable 2023 fact.","ruler_attribution":"No specific conduct by AMLO is established in the supplied units.","limitations":["No material fact about AMLO or Mexico’s 2023 journalist safety situation can be extracted from the supplied units."]},{"source_id":"SRC-81ab26f8c028af05","start_unit":3,"end_unit":4,"fact_summary":"A 2018 TIME profile described AMLO’s stated program as reviving poorer pueblos through roads, school repairs, pensions, subsidies, anti-corruption and bureaucracy cuts, support for small farmers, food self-sufficiency, and a peace plan for drug violence; it also described his grassroots network, nationalist state-led economic orientation, and critics’ concerns that presidential decision-making and populist conflict with elites could endanger democratic checks.","question_ids":["2B.3","3B.6","4B.2","4B.3","4B.5","5B.1","5B.6","6B.1","6B.3","7B.8","8B.1","8B.3"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"Pre-presidential 2018 campaign evidence used only to identify AMLO’s stated program and governing style; it does not demonstrate 2023 implementation or outcomes.","ruler_attribution":"The profile directly reports AMLO’s promises, political organization, and critics’ assessments.","limitations":["The source predates the 2023 target period by five years.","Promises and third-party expectations are not evidence that the policies were enacted, funded, or effective."]},{"source_id":"SRC-ee93bbc8399ea76f","start_unit":20,"end_unit":22,"fact_summary":"CPJ reported that from March 2023 AMLO repeatedly criticized Article 19, Proceso, Animal Político, Aristegui Noticias, and reporter Nayeli Roldán over coverage of alleged illegal government spyware use; he called Roldán unobjective, unprofessional, and part of bribed media, accused Article 19 of U.S. government funding, and did not correct disputed claims. The targeted journalists and organizations reported increased online abuse, misogynistic comments, threats, stalking, and safety concerns; CPJ also reported that Mexico was the Western Hemisphere’s deadliest country for journalists in 2022.","question_ids":["3B.3","3B.8","3B.9","4B.3","4B.6","4B.9","6B.5","7B.1","7B.2","7B.7","7B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"Directly concerns AMLO’s public conduct in 2023; the journalist-killing comparison is a 2022 contextual baseline.","ruler_attribution":"The statements and criticisms are attributed directly to AMLO; reported threats and safety effects are attributed to journalists and CPJ sources.","limitations":["The supplied text reports alleged spyware evidence and reactions but does not establish a final judicial finding on the surveillance.","The causal link between AMLO’s statements and individual online threats is reported by affected parties and CPJ, not independently adjudicated in the supplied units."]},{"source_id":"SRC-fe48f5931dd897a5","start_unit":2,"end_unit":4,"fact_summary":"In September 2023 AMLO transferred control of the Mayan Train to SEDENA and had already transferred ports, airports, and rail administration to the military, creating military-controlled companies and infrastructure operators. The stated rationale was reducing corruption and ensuring timely completion, but critics cited limited relevant military expertise, weak transparency and accountability, risks of concealed information and impunity, Indigenous-community disruption and militarization, and a Mayan Train cost increase from an initial $7.2 billion estimate to more than $28 billion.","question_ids":["3B.2","3B.7","4B.4","4B.5","4B.6","5B.4","5B.5","5B.6","5B.7","6B.3","6B.4","6B.5","7B.3","7B.5","7B.6","7B.7","7B.9","8B.2","8B.3","8B.4","8B.5","8B.6","8B.7","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"Directly concerns institutional and infrastructure decisions made or operating in 2023, with some project history from 2020–2022.","ruler_attribution":"The transfers and presidential decree are attributed to AMLO; criticism and cost estimates are attributed to activists, academics, and cited organizations.","limitations":["The article is based substantially on interviews and advocacy/academic criticism and does not provide a complete audited account of project costs or performance.","The supplied evidence does not establish final project benefits, profitability, or the full legal scope of oversight."]},{"source_id":"SRC-46059cc67086bef1","start_unit":6,"end_unit":8,"fact_summary":"Mexico’s INE reported that the 2022 presidential recall process was conducted with all polling stations installed, 57,449 acts counted, and 16,502,636 participants; 91.86% voted for AMLO to remain and 6.44% for removal, below the 40% participation threshold required for a binding result. INE also reported 51 precautionary measures, 18 noncompliance agreements involving public officials, and that the electoral authority transmitted certified records to the Electoral Tribunal and notified the presidency.","question_ids":["4B.1","4B.2","4B.4","4B.8","4B.10","7B.6","7B.7","8B.9"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The process occurred in 2022, providing institutional and constitutional context relevant to AMLO’s position and accountability during 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The result concerned AMLO’s presidency; the supplied text attributes administration, enforcement, and certification to INE and does not state AMLO’s compliance or obstruction beyond the institutional context.","limitations":["The source is an INE institutional account and does not independently assess AMLO’s conduct toward the process.","It provides no 2023 election or succession event."]},{"source_id":"SRC-e10784a7cf4261ae","start_unit":6,"end_unit":9,"fact_summary":"Brookings described AMLO’s announced 2018–2024 security plan as combining root-cause policies, anti-corruption, human-rights protections, public-health measures, transitional justice, prison and security-sector reform, and a National Guard, but judged key elements unclear and unlikely to reduce violence quickly. It reported delayed or inadequate anti-corruption and prosecutorial appointments, refusal to support an autonomous attorney-general selection, continued military domestic law enforcement, opaque National Guard deployment logic, weak police reform, and unresolved risks around amnesty, militias, and drug-licensing enforcement, while viewing alternative livelihoods and a human-rights-centered strategy as potentially positive.","question_ids":["2B.1","2B.3","2B.4","2B.5","2B.6","2B.9","3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.5","3B.6","3B.9","4B.4","4B.5","5B.5","6B.1","6B.6","7B.5","7B.6","7B.7","8B.1","8B.2","8B.3","8B.4","8B.5","8B.6","8B.7","8B.8","8B.9"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"Published in 2019 and therefore predictive/background evidence about the administration’s program and implementation risks, not a direct 2023 evaluation.","ruler_attribution":"The analysis explicitly evaluates AMLO’s announced strategy and administrative choices.","limitations":["The source substantially predates 2023 and does not establish later implementation, adaptation, or outcomes.","Brookings states that the publication represents the author’s views; several conclusions are forecasts or recommendations rather than verified results."]},{"source_id":"SRC-83e51281affeb96f","start_unit":17,"end_unit":20,"fact_summary":"International IDEA’s Mexico profile reports mid-range performance in Representation, Rights, and Participation but low-range Rule of Law, with declines since 2019 in Credible Elections, Civil Liberties, Freedom of the Press, Freedom of Movement, and Judicial Independence. It describes poverty affecting over 36% of the population, structural discrimination against Indigenous peoples, concerning gender-based violence, persistent drug-related violence, and criticism that executive media/opposition attacks and reforms of autonomous institutions weakened democratic checks; it also notes that Morena’s platform and anti-corruption/austerity priorities were highly popular.","question_ids":["3B.3","3B.6","3B.7","3B.8","4B.2","4B.3","4B.4","4B.6","4B.7","4B.9","4B.10","5B.8","6B.3","6B.8","6B.10","7B.10","8B.7","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The profile was last updated in 2025 and summarizes trends since 2019; it is relevant to the 2023 period but is not a contemporaneous 2023-only assessment.","ruler_attribution":"The profile attributes the executive criticism, institutional reform initiatives, and Morena policy priorities to the AMLO-era government, while some conditions are national or inherited.","limitations":["The supplied profile includes post-2023 developments and cannot isolate AMLO’s 2023 responsibility for every indicator.","The units provide categorical/trend descriptions rather than a full 2023 statistical series or causal evaluation."]}],"documents_with_no_material_fact":[],"batch_limitations":["The supplied documents vary substantially in period: several are background or post-2023 sources rather than 2023-only evidence.","No source supplied direct evidence on nuclear weapons, arms control, proliferation, or other existential-risk governance; those questions are therefore not substantively supported by the extracted materials.","Facts are reported without scoring, and source criticism or uncertainty is recorded in limitations rather than converted into ratings."]}
